rows.claim: Capacity is typically around 24,000 litres, and they are built either as a single vessel or divided into three or four sectional compartments

rows.note: AWRI publishes 0.8-1.3 g/L for white table wines and <0.5 g/L for reds. The claim's white band runs 100 mg/L high at the top and its red band (300-600) straddles a ceiling AWRI puts at 500.

rows.claim: crossflow or a 0.65 micrometre membrane

source.quote: Surface filters such as membrane filters are used as a final filter to remove smaller microorganisms... The 'bubble point' is the gas pressure at which the surface tension of water in the pores of a saturated filter is overcome... 0.65 um membrane: 20.3 psig (140 kPa); 0.45 um membrane: 26.1 psig (180 kPa). Most cross-flow membranes are only nominally rated at 0.2 um which is theoretically tight enough for sterile filtration.

rows.note: Both routes are recognised by AWRI; note its caveat that cross-flow membranes are only NOMINALLY rated at 0.2 um and cannot be integrity-tested, so a nominal cross-flow pass is not equivalent to an absolute-rated sterile membrane.

rows.claim: a heat test at 80

source.quote: Heat the sample at 80 C for two hours. While six hours has been typical industry practice for the heat test, recent research has shown that two hours of [heating is sufficient]... | White wine | 2 hours | 3 hours | < 2.0 NTU |

rows.note: 80 degrees C is correct and the claim wisely omits a duration - AWRI's current protocol is 2 hours heating and 3 hours cooling, not the older 6 hours.

rows.claim: a cold test at minus 4

source.ref: Carboxymethylcellulose FAQ / Measurement of cold stability of wine (AWRI)
source.quote: The AWRI recommends that cold stability be determined by storing a filtered 150 mL aliquot of wine at -4 C for three days, and then examining it for the presence of a crystalline deposit.

rows.note: Exact match to AWRI's recommended brine/cold test: -4 degrees C for three days (72 hours) on a filtered 150 mL aliquot.

rows.claim: loading temperature at or below 15
rows.note: AWRI's 15 degrees C is a bottling/sparging compromise temperature, and WSU reports <15 degrees C limits Brettanomyces growth in combination with molecular SO2 - neither is a published bulk-loading specification. The figure is defensible by analogy but not sourced as written.

rows.claim: Regulation (EC) 178/2002

source.publisher: EUR-Lex - Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 (General Food Law), Articles 18-19
source.quote: The traceability of food, feed, food-producing animals, and any other substance intended to be... incorporated into a food or feed shall be established at all stages of production, processing and distribution... [operators] shall immediately initiate procedures to withdraw the food in question from the market

rows.note: Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 (the General Food Law) is correctly cited: Article 18 imposes traceability at all stages, Article 19 requires immediate withdrawal and notification of the competent authority where food may be unsafe. Both obligations are exactly what a glass-in-bottle complaint triggers.
